name: Enlighten laser

lead: Enlighten is a laser platform from Cutera used in clinics to target pigment in the skin, including tattoo ink and pigmented spots. The pulse is extremely short, so energy shatters pigment particles that the body then clears.

For appearance, it is used to clear unwanted tattoos and pigmentation for a more even skin tone. Wikipedia describes picosecond lasers only briefly, as a recent area with anecdotal claims of faster clearance.

paras: A trained provider treats the area over multiple sessions spaced weeks apart. The number of sessions depends on the pigment and skin.
Temporary pigment changes occur in about half of laser tattoo removal patients, usually resolving within 6 to 12 months; darker skin has higher risk of pigmentation changes.

web.title: Picosecond lasers for tattoo removal: a systematic review
Comparing laser treatments in tattoo removal
Systematic Review of Picosecond Laser in Dermatology

chain: Ultra-short laser pulse absorbed by pigment
Pigment fragments cleared by the body
angle.text: The laser targets pigment itself, lightening tattoos and dark spots across a course of treatments.

lead: Enlighten is an aesthetic laser platform marketed by Cutera for clinic use on pigment concerns, chiefly unwanted tattoos and pigmented spots. People use treatments of this kind to lighten or clear ink and dark marks so skin tone looks more even.[1]

Lasers of this type work by delivering very short pulses that fragment pigment particles in the skin; the body's immune system then clears the fragments over the following weeks. Conventional tattoo-removal systems use nanosecond-range (Q-switched) pulses, while picosecond-class systems use shorter ones, a newer area in which Wikipedia notes a picosecond version of the 755 nm alexandrite wavelength and anecdotal claims of faster ink clearance.[1] Frequency-doubled 532 nm Nd:YAG light is strongly absorbed by melanin and is used for age spots and sun spots.[1]

Published reviews of picosecond lasers as a category exist: a 2016 systematic review of tattoo removal and later reviews in dermatology are summarised below.[2][3][4][5] No published trials were located that test Enlighten by name.

paras: Tattoo ink and melanin absorb short laser pulses, and the resulting photoacoustic shock fragments the particles; very short pulses limit heat spread into surrounding skin.[1] Different wavelengths suit different colours. Wikipedia lists 532 nm as best for red and orange, 694 nm for blue, 755 nm for green and also for black and blue to a lesser degree, and 1064 nm (poorly absorbed by melanin) as the wavelength of choice for darker skin and black ink.[1]
Multi-wavelength platforms, which have been sold since about 2006, treat more ink colours but with less power at each wavelength.[1]

The practical appearance goals are fading or removing a tattoo (for example one that no longer matches a person's look, or a poorly done one) and reducing dark spots such as sun spots or age spots so skin looks more uniform.[1] Treatments are given in clinic by a trained provider over several sessions; Wikipedia says tattoo sessions are typically spaced eight or more weeks apart and that outcomes depend on skin colour, ink colour and ink depth. Black and dark inks often clear fully, while yellows and greens are hard to remove, and professional tattoos tend to clear more easily than amateur ones.[1]

The Kirby-Desai scale is a scoring system used to estimate how many sessions a tattoo may need, and tattoos on extremities such as the ankle generally take longest.[1] Many patients describe the procedure as more painful than getting the tattoo, and clinics use topical anaesthetic, cooling or injected lidocaine.[1]

Picosecond lasers have been studied extensively as a category. A 2016 systematic review in Lasers in Medical Science included eight trials (six in humans, 160 participants in total) and reported that 69 to 100 percent of tattoos reached more than 70 percent pigment clearance after one to ten treatments; it described evidence that picosecond beat nanosecond lasers as sparse, mainly for black and blue tattoos, with minor side effects.[2]

A 2022 systematic review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology covered 36 studies (seven randomised trials, two non-randomised controlled trials and 27 case series). It reported Q-switched Nd:YAG lasers as safe and effective, picosecond lasers performing better on blue, green and yellow pigments, and both types working for black tattoos; the authors noted variability between studies and a need for more randomised trials.[3]

A 2021 review of 77 studies in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine rated the evidence by indication, with tattoo removal at the highest evidence level, and concluded picosecond lasers were safe and effective for a growing range of dermatologic uses including benign pigmented lesions, rejuvenation, melasma and scar revision.[4] A 2019 Dermatologic Surgery review of 27 studies from 1988 to 2017 listed tattoo removal, benign pigmented lesions, acne scarring and photoaging as indications.[5]

About half of laser tattoo-removal patients have transient pigment changes that usually resolve in 6 to 12 months; hyperpigmentation is more common in skin types IV to VI and hypopigmentation more common in darker skin. Scarring and texture change are rare, blistering very rare, and allergic reactions to ink can occur.[1] Some inks, particularly white, flesh-tone and pink, can darken paradoxically after treatment, and a crust that forms usually sheds around two weeks later and should not be picked, since early removal raises scarring risk.[1]
Wikipedia also notes a theoretical concern that breakdown of azo dyes could release aromatic amines.[1]

Short-pulse laser effects on tattoos were first reported by Leon Goldman and colleagues in the late 1960s; CO2 and argon lasers were tried in 1978 and 1979 with scarring and limited success, and Q-switched ruby lasers were studied in Glasgow from the early 1980s.[1] Q-switched systems became commercially practical in the late 1980s, and a Massachusetts General Hospital group published one of the first American reports in 1990.[1] Picosecond systems followed as a later development.[1][5]
No studies found of Enlighten specifically. Studies of picosecond lasers in general are described above.[2][3][4][5]

timeline.event: Leon Goldman and others first report short-pulse laser effects on tattoos.[1]
Q-switched ruby lasers for blue and black tattoos studied in Glasgow.[1]
Massachusetts General Hospital group publishes one of the first American articles on Q-switched tattoo removal.[1]
Multi-wavelength tattoo-removal systems begin to appear.[1]
Systematic review of picosecond lasers for tattoo removal published in Lasers in Medical Science.[2]
Systematic review of 77 picosecond laser studies in dermatology published.[4]
JAAD systematic review compares laser treatments for tattoo removal.[3]
